summary:
Chukotka Autonomous Okrug stands under the national framework of Russia, and the sources assembled for this unit contain no division-specific trans-related findings. All three records are national in scope: a foreign-government country policy note, a travel advisory and a nationwide human-rights report. The prohibitions a trans visitor would encounter in Anadyr are the ones that apply across the Russian Federation, legislated by the national parliament and enforced by national courts and security services.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) sets out the baseline. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned, and the constitution offers no specific legal protections for LGBT+ people. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were prohibited outright in 2023, when the law banning gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes took effect; the note records trans-specific healthcare as effectively banned that year.

Public expression promoting non-heterosexual relationships or gender transition falls under the 'gay propaganda' law, which carries fines of up to 400,000 rubles or up to 15 days' detention, with repeated offences risking criminal prosecution. The expanded statute reaches anything that publicly 'justifies' gender transition, so a visitor's own accounts, posts or visible presentation can constitute the offence.

Foreigners face the sharper end of the regime. The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, advises against all travel regardless of personal characteristics, and warns that foreigners found guilty under the propaganda law may be arrested, detained for up to 15 days and deported. Displaying certain symbols, explicitly including the rainbow flag, is itself a crime.

Since the Supreme Court designated the 'international LGBT movement' an extremist organisation in November 2023, the charges have carried prison terms. Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions for participating in that movement or displaying its symbols as of 30 June 2025, with sentences of up to 12 years. The same report documents 81 people found guilty in 98 administrative cases since January 2024 under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols, most of them on social media, and 257 'gay propaganda' penalties imposed in 2023-24 against 22 in the preceding two years. Between 2022 and 2024 the Home Office note counts at least 139 individuals affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement.

Physical harm accompanies the legal exposure. Masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars within 48 hours of the extremist designation, ordering about 100 patrons at one venue to face walls for search and photography. In December 2024 a Russian man held on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility, and a transgender woman was held for nine months at a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk and forced to take testosterone before escaping. Nothing in the sources indicates that Chukotka Autonomous Okrug is insulated from these practices.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement is rising in volume as well as severity. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget across the two preceding years, a scale of routine penalty that sits alongside the much smaller number of prison terms.

The speed of the crackdown after the Supreme Court ruling was documented by The Guardian on 17 January 2024: at least three venues were raided the same night in Moscow, and the pattern of raids, arrests and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025, according to The Moscow Times (23 June 2025), which quoted a St Petersburg queer woman describing herself as a second-class citizen under the designation.

The Home Office note treats LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, as constituting a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia. Both point to protection machinery that operates outside the jurisdiction rather than within it.

The trajectory since 2022 is one of deterioration rather than a fixed position: the 2023 bans on legal recognition and healthcare, the November 2023 extremist designation and the widening of the propaganda statute are sequential measures, and a visitor's exposure depends on how each is applied at the time of travel.
localsOnly:
Residents of Chukotka Autonomous Okrug are subject to the same national codes as visitors, without the additional lever of deportation. Administrative liability under article 20.3 for displaying banned symbols has been applied mostly on social media, which makes ordinary online posting the most common route to a charge, while repeat propaganda offences escalate into criminal proceedings.

At least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement between 2022 and 2024, and 257 propaganda penalties were imposed in 2023-24, so the enforcement burden falls overwhelmingly on people living in the country rather than on travellers. Sentences of up to 12 years are available under the extremism provisions.

With legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care prohibited since 2023, residents have no domestic route to update documents or obtain trans-specific medical treatment. Same-sex marriage is unavailable and the constitution supplies no specific legal protection.

The sources contain no information on local support services, shelters, community organisations or police practice within Chukotka Autonomous Okrug itself; nothing indicates whether any division-level accommodation exists.
outOfScopeNotes:
No division-specific reporting on Chukotka Autonomous Okrug was located. The presence or absence of raids, extremism charges, arrests or document-refusal cases within this unit is unresolved: the three sources are national, and the Home Office note itself contains no division-level detail beyond the national framework.

Whether national security services operate in this unit with the same intensity as in the major urban centres is not sourced. Nor is the practical treatment of a foreign trans traveller at the border here specifically documented; the entry-screening and document-check experience for this unit is not covered by the inventory.

Local facility availability, including any gender-affirming providers or trans-competent healthcare, is not sourced and should be treated as unknown rather than absent. The same applies to any division-level protection mechanism, complaint route or community organisation.

The conversion-therapy case reported by BBC Russian (27 July 2024) occurred near Novosibirsk and is used here only as evidence of a nationwide pattern of physical coercion against transgender people; it is not a Chukotka finding, and no comparable case from this unit was located.
